opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of those ideas that sounds a bit boring but could actually matter quite a lot. The basic intuition is that if something goes wrong with AI, or if we're worried something *might* be going wrong, one of the most useful things you can have is a record of what actually happened. What were the models asked to do, what did they do, and who was using them?

There are a few different risks where this seems helpful. One is misuse. If someone is using a model to get serious uplift on, say, a bioweapons project or a large-scale cyberattack, it's a lot easier to notice patterns, investigate after the fact, and deter people in the first place if there's a reasonable expectation that interactions are retained and can be looked at under appropriate conditions. Deterrence is underrated here. You don't need to catch everyone; you need people to believe there's a real chance of getting caught.

Another is the misalignment side. If models are being deployed as agents doing long chains of actions in the world, and at some point we start seeing weird behavior, like a model that seems to be sandbagging, deceiving its overseers, or quietly pursuing some goal nobody intended, you really want to be able to go back and study that. Logs are kind of the raw material for learning what our AI systems are actually doing in the wild, as opposed to what they do in a carefully constructed eval.

Now, I don't want to pretend this is free. There are real privacy concerns. People are putting extremely sensitive stuff into these systems: medical questions, legal issues, personal relationships, business secrets. So I wouldn't advocate "keep everything forever and let anyone look at it." I'd think about things like: retaining logs for a defined period, with strong access controls; having clear, narrow conditions under which humans can review them; maybe using automated classifiers to flag a small fraction of concerning activity rather than having people read through things broadly; and being transparent with users about what the policy is.

I'd also distinguish between consumer chat and higher-stakes settings. If a model has access to powerful tools, can take actions on the internet, run code, move money, then the case for detailed logging gets a lot stronger, sort of the way we expect audit trails in finance or in sensitive government systems.

And the last thing I'd say is that this is the kind of measure that's relatively cheap to put in place now and potentially very hard to retrofit later. If we end up in a world where we're trying to figure out whether some AI incident was misuse, an accident, or a model acting on its own, and the answer is "well, nobody kept the records," that would be a pretty painful place to be. So I think of it as part of a broader package of building the basic visibility and infrastructure we're going to want, even if we're uncertain exactly which risks end up mattering most.

r002.rationale: It explicitly proposes retaining logs for a defined period as a privacy-conscious safeguard.

r003.rationale: It does not propose offering customers additional AI usage in exchange for sharing interaction data.

r004.rationale: It frames logging as useful for visibility and investigating incidents, but does not connect it to the political feasibility of sweeping AI risk regulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of those things that I think is really underrated, and it's a good example of a category I keep coming back to, which is: what are the things that are cheap, that are not very controversial, that you could do now, and that would put us in a much better position later when the stakes are higher?

So the basic idea is just: when an AI system is deployed and it's doing things in the world — it's writing code, it's sending emails, it's taking actions on behalf of some company — you keep a record of what it did. The inputs it got, the outputs it produced, the actions it took. And you keep that record for some reasonable period of time, and you have some process by which, if something goes wrong, people can actually go back and look at it.

And the reason I think this matters is that a lot of my worries about AI are worries about things that are hard to notice. If an AI system is doing something subtly bad — it's sabotaging some safety research, it's inserting a vulnerability into some code, it's manipulating someone — the thing that would make that catastrophic is if it happens and nobody ever finds out. Whereas if it happens and there's a record, then you have the chance to catch it, to understand it, and crucially, to learn from it. You can go, "Okay, this model did this thing, that's really concerning, let's figure out why, let's change how we train the next one."

I sometimes think about this by analogy to other fields. Aviation has an incident reporting culture, where near-misses get documented and investigated, and that's a huge part of why flying is so safe. And you can't do any of that if you don't have the black box. You can't learn from the incident if there's no record of the incident.

Now, there are real tensions here. The obvious one is privacy. People are putting all kinds of sensitive stuff into these systems, and "we're going to retain everything forever" is not a great answer. So I think you want to be thoughtful about it — things like retention periods that aren't indefinite, access controls so it's not just anyone poking through the logs, maybe a focus on the agentic, high-stakes uses rather than every chat about someone's dinner recipe. I don't think the answer is "log everything with no safeguards," I think the answer is "don't throw away the evidence you'd need to investigate a serious incident."

The other thing I'd say is that this is also a case where I think it's really valuable to get the norm established early. Right now the stakes are relatively low, the systems are relatively limited, and it's a lot easier to build the habit and the infrastructure than it will be later, when there's much more at stake and more resistance to anything that looks like oversight. If you wait until there's a clear catastrophe and then say "we need logging," you've already lost the ability to investigate that catastrophe.

So I'd put it in the bucket of: not a silver bullet, not going to solve alignment, but a pretty basic hygiene measure that makes a lot of the other things we might want to do — incident response, accountability, actually learning about how these systems fail — possible at all. And I think it's one of the better candidates for something that could be done through policy relatively soon without needing to resolve the really hard questions first.

astra-6.text:
I think retaining logs of AI interactions could be a pretty valuable part of understanding and managing the risks. If something goes wrong, you want to be able to investigate what happened. And even before something goes wrong, you want some ability to look for warning signs and check whether your safety measures are working.

But I’d distinguish retaining logs from giving lots of people access to them. Those interactions can contain extremely sensitive information. So you’d want strong security, tight limits on who can access the logs and for what purposes, and a thoughtful policy on how long to keep them.

I don’t have a precise retention period to propose. I’d want to understand what information is actually useful for detecting dangerous behavior or investigating an incident, and weigh that against the privacy and security costs. It seems like a useful accountability measure, but it’s one piece of a much larger approach to AI safety.

r001.rationale: The response discusses security and retention policy but does not identify organizational policy, rather than technical feasibility, as the obstacle.

r002.rationale: It says retention duration should be considered, but does not propose time-limited retention as a compromise with privacy or business concerns.

r003.rationale: It does not propose exchanging additional AI usage for customers’ voluntary data sharing.

r004.rationale: It calls logs an accountability measure, but does not connect them to the political feasibility of sweeping AI risk regulation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s worth distinguishing between keeping logs and making them available to someone. You could retain records of what an AI system did without giving a government, or the public, routine access to everyone’s conversations. Those are very different decisions, and the privacy implications matter a lot.

The case for keeping some records is that, if something goes wrong, we’d like to be able to reconstruct what happened. Was someone deliberately using the system to cause harm? Did the system behave in a way its developers didn’t anticipate? Were there warning signs? If the relevant records are gone, it may be very hard to answer those questions or prevent a repeat.

But I wouldn’t jump from that to ‘retain everything forever.’ I’d want to know which records actually help us investigate serious incidents, how long we need them, and what safeguards govern access. Logs themselves can contain extremely sensitive information, and collecting them creates risks too.

So I’d see this as a potentially useful piece of accountability and incident investigation. I wouldn’t see it as a substitute for figuring out whether a system is safe before deploying it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether and how long to retain logs, but does not identify organizational policy as the obstacle or contrast it with technical feasibility.

r002.rationale: It proposes deciding how long records are needed and rejects keeping everything forever, balancing investigative value against privacy risks.

r003.rationale: It does not suggest offering customers additional AI usage in exchange for voluntarily sharing data.

r004.rationale: It describes logs as useful for accountability and incident investigation, but does not connect them to the political feasibility of sweeping AI risk regulation.
